people/john-of-the-cross/summary: Spanish Carmelite friar who joined Teresa's reform and was imprisoned by his own order. His poems and commentaries — The Dark Night of the Soul, Ascent of Mount Carmel, Spiritual Canticle — describe purgation and union with God through faith beyond images.
people/matteo-ricci/summary: Italian Jesuit who entered China in 1582 and lived in Beijing from 1601. Adopting the dress and learning of Confucian scholars, he wrote The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, made a famous world map and translated Euclid with Xu Guangqi. His accommodation of ancestral rites was later condemned.
people/jacobus-arminius/summary: Dutch Reformed pastor and Leiden professor, trained under Beza, who came to teach that God elects those he foresees will believe, that grace may be resisted and that Christ died for all. His followers' Remonstrance was condemned at Dort; Arminian theology later shaped Methodism and much of evangelicalism.
people/cyril-lucaris/summary: Cretan-born patriarch of Alexandria and then Constantinople, who sought Protestant allies against Jesuit influence and published a Confession with Calvinist doctrines (1629). Repeatedly deposed and restored by Ottoman politics, he was strangled in 1638; Orthodox synods condemned the Confession.
people/hugo-grotius/summary: Dutch prodigy and Remonstrant sympathiser imprisoned after Dort, who escaped in a book chest. His On the Law of War and Peace founded international law, and his defence of the satisfaction of Christ developed the 'governmental' theory of the atonement.
people/cornelius-jansen/summary: Flemish theologian and bishop of Ypres whose posthumous Augustinus (1640) argued for Augustine's strong doctrine of efficacious grace against Jesuit theologians. Five propositions attributed to it were condemned in 1653; 'Jansenism' became a rigorist movement centred on Port-Royal.
people/rose-of-lima/summary: Isabel Flores de Oliva, a Dominican tertiary in Lima known for severe penances, care for the poor and sick, and mystical prayer. Canonised in 1671, she was the first saint born in the Americas and is patroness of Latin America.
people/richard-baxter/summary: Puritan pastor whose ministry transformed Kidderminster through catechising households. A moderate who sought unity, he was ejected in 1662 and later imprisoned. The Reformed Pastor and The Saints' Everlasting Rest made him one of the most widely read devotional writers.
people/john-owen/summary: Leading Puritan theologian, chaplain to Cromwell and vice-chancellor of Oxford, later an Independent pastor in London. His The Death of Death in the Death of Christ defends particular redemption; other works treat communion with the Trinity, mortification of sin and the Holy Spirit.
people/blaise-pascal/summary: French mathematician and physicist who, after a night of fire in November 1654 recorded in his Memorial, devoted himself to faith in association with Port-Royal. His Provincial Letters satirised Jesuit casuistry, and his unfinished apology, the Pensées, includes the famous 'wager'.
people/george-fox/summary: English weaver's son and seeker who in 1647 heard 'There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition'. He founded the Religious Society of Friends, preaching the Inward Light, rejecting steeple-houses, tithes and oaths; he was imprisoned repeatedly and travelled to America and the Netherlands.
people/george-fox/keyIdeas/1: No professional clergy or outward sacraments
people/philipp-jakob-spener/summary: Lutheran pastor at Frankfurt, Dresden and Berlin, often called the father of Pietism. His Pia Desideria (1675) proposed Bible study groups, lay priesthood, practical faith and heartfelt preaching to renew a church he saw as formal and quarrelsome.
people/jacob-ammann/summary: Swiss Brethren elder in Alsace whose call for strict social shunning, twice-yearly communion with foot-washing and plain dress led to the division of 1693. His followers, the Amish, later settled in Pennsylvania and spread across North America.
people/bartholomaus-ziegenbalg/summary: German Pietist from Halle sent by the Danish king to Tranquebar in 1706, the first Protestant missionary in India. He mastered Tamil, translated the New Testament (1714), founded schools and a printing press, and wrote sympathetic studies of South Indian religion.
people/kimpa-vita/summary: A Kongolese noblewoman who in 1704 announced she had died and been possessed by St Anthony, preaching that Christ and Mary were Kongolese and calling for the kingdom's reunification. Her Antonian movement drew thousands to the ruined capital; condemned by Capuchins, she was burned in 1706.
people/kimpa-vita/keyIdeas/1: Political and spiritual renewal of Kongo
people/nicolaus-zinzendorf/summary: Saxon nobleman raised in Halle Pietism who sheltered Moravian refugees at Herrnhut and became their bishop. His 'religion of the heart' centred on the wounds of the Lamb; he launched worldwide missions and founded settlements such as Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.
people/nicolaus-zinzendorf/keyIdeas/0: Heart religion centred on Christ's wounds
people/jonathan-edwards/summary: New England Congregationalist pastor whose Northampton revival (1734–35) and writings — A Faithful Narrative, Religious Affections, Freedom of the Will — made him the theologian of the Great Awakening. Dismissed by his church in 1750, he served as missionary to the Mohicans at Stockbridge and died as president of Princeton. He also enslaved people, a fact now prominently discussed.
people/jonathan-edwards/keyIdeas/0: Religious affections as mark of true religion
people/john-wesley/summary: Anglican priest whose heart was 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate in 1738. Riding some 250,000 miles, he preached in the open air and organised converts into societies, classes and bands, creating Methodism. He taught universal grace, assurance and Christian perfection (entire sanctification) and opposed slavery.
people/charles-wesley/summary: John's younger brother, converted days before him in May 1738, who wrote some 6,000 hymns including 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing' and 'And Can It Be'. His hymns taught Methodist theology to ordinary believers; he remained firmly loyal to the Church of England.
people/george-whitefield/summary: Anglican evangelist whose dramatic open-air preaching drew crowds of tens of thousands in Britain and the American colonies, uniting the First Great Awakening. A Calvinist Methodist, he differed from Wesley on predestination. He also defended slavery in Georgia, a stain on his legacy.
people/paisius-velichkovsky/summary: Ukrainian monk who lived on Mount Athos and later led large communities in Moldavia at Dragomirna and Neamț. His Slavonic translation of the Philokalia (1793) spread hesychast prayer and spiritual eldership through Russia, inspiring the startsy of Optina.
people/yi-seung-hun/summary: A Korean Confucian scholar who, after studying Catholic books, was baptised in Beijing in 1784 as Peter and returned to found a lay-led church in Korea. He was beheaded in the Sinyu persecution of 1801.
people/william-wilberforce/summary: Member of Parliament for Yorkshire whose evangelical conversion (1785) led him, with the Clapham Sect, Quakers and Black abolitionists, to campaign for abolition of the slave trade, achieved in 1807. He died days after the Slavery Abolition Act passed in 1833.
people/william-carey/summary: English shoemaker and Baptist pastor whose Enquiry (1792) helped found the Baptist Missionary Society. In India from 1793, he and colleagues at Serampore translated the Bible into dozens of languages, founded Serampore College and campaigned against sati. He is often called 'the father of modern missions'.
people/friedrich-schleiermacher/summary: Prussian Reformed theologian raised among the Moravians, often called the father of modern liberal theology. His Speeches on Religion and The Christian Faith ground doctrine in the 'feeling of absolute dependence' on God and reinterpret it in relation to Christ's God-consciousness.
people/friedrich-schleiermacher/keyIdeas: Religion as feeling of absolute dependence
Doctrine as expression of Christian experience
people/william-miller/summary: Baptist farmer-preacher who calculated from Daniel 8:14 that Christ would return around 1843–44. His movement drew perhaps 50,000–100,000 followers; after the Great Disappointment of 22 October 1844 he acknowledged his error but kept hoping for an imminent return.
people/robert-morrison/summary: London Missionary Society missionary, the first Protestant missionary in China (1807). Working under East India Company restrictions, he translated the Bible into Chinese with William Milne and compiled a monumental Chinese–English dictionary.
